newsitem.title: USA: Beijing says Hong Kong aids Taiwan reunification.
newsitem.headline: Beijing says Hong Kong aids Taiwan reunification.

text.p: Hong Kong's return to Chinese sovereignty could lay the groundwork for reunification with Taiwan, Chinese vice premier Zhu Rongji told Newsweek magazine in an interview released on Sunday.

"I firmly believe that the successful implementation of one country, two systems will surely contribute to reunification," Zhu said in an exclusive interview in the news magazine's latest edition, due out on Monday.

"Our terms for Taiwan's return to the motherland are more generous," Zhu said. "We will not deploy troops or station troops on Taiwan, and Taiwan's leaders can come to be leaders in the central government. But as for when Taiwan will return to the motherland, it will be when forces in the U.S. no longer support an independent Taiwan."
Communist-ruled China has regarded Taiwan as a rebel province since 1949, when defeated Nationalist forces took refuge on the island after years of civil war.

Beijing, which reserves the right to invade Taiwan if it ever declares formal independence, has repeatedly demanded the island's leaders accept the principle of "One China" and prove their intention to eventually reunify with the mainland.
Zhu, the architect of China's economic reforms, reiterated Beijing's stance to its military option against Taiwan.
While he maintains that "it is our consistent policy that we will achieve reunification through peaceful means," he added "we will not give up the military option."

He said missile tests conducted by China off the coast of Taiwan last year were "normal exercises" and probably did not discourage Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui in his push for independence. "I don't think he will really pull back when he can purchase and import advanced weapons from the U.S. at will," he added.

In a wide-ranging interview with Newsweek editor Maynard Parker in Beijing, Zhu also said there would be minimal interference by China's central government in Hong Kong after the handover from Britain in July.

"Except for defense and foreign affairs, the central government of China won't interfere in Hong Kong's internal affairs and will pursue the policy of one country, two systems ... the facts will show that it will be successfully implemented," Zhu said.
He added, however, that Hong Kong's current success and development was due not only to its political system.
"Hong Kong's success is mainly determined by Hong Kong's people. But without development in China, Hong Kong would not have enjoyed the level of development that it has today."
